summary: Defines a set of extended status codes for the mail system, used in delivery status reports, tracking and diagnostics. Together with Delivery Status Notifications, they allow delivery results to be shown in a way that does not depend on language or media.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3463 defines detailed codes that mail systems can use to report delivery results. Each code says whether delivery succeeded, what part of the system was involved, and what condition occurred.

subtitle: A three-part status code that reports mail delivery results in a machine-readable, language-independent form.

tldr.problem: SMTP reply codes and system-specific text do not provide enough detail for consistent, language-independent delivery reports.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3463 defines codes in the form class.subject.detail. The class indicates success or failure, the subject groups the likely source, and the detail identifies a more specific condition.
tldr.outcome: It is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1893 and has been updated by RFC 3886, RFC 4468, RFC 4865, RFC 4954, and RFC 5248.

today: RFC 3463 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1893. It has been updated by RFC 3886, RFC 4468, RFC 4865, RFC 4954, and RFC 5248.

sections.title: Why Mail Needs Enhanced Status Codes
sections.content:
Mail delivery reports need a standard way to describe errors in more detail than SMTP reply codes or system-specific text. RFC 3463 defines enhanced status codes for delivery status notifications, tracking, and diagnostics. The codes are intended to support reporting that does not depend on a particular language or display medium.

The RFC says SMTP has about 12 useful codes for delivery reports, and each can refer to several different conditions. Reusing the remaining SMTP reply-code space would also limit room for future ESMTP extensions. The enhanced codes use a separate structure based on the broad success and failure meanings of SMTP replies.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail systems need more detail than a short SMTP reply can provide. Enhanced status codes give delivery reports a shared way to describe what happened.

sections.title: The Three Parts of a Status Code
sections.content:
A status code has three numeric fields separated by periods: class, subject, and detail. The class is 2, 4, or 5; subject and detail each contain one to three digits. A code has no spaces, comments, or leading zeroes within its numeric subcodes. The RFC gives 2.1.23 as an example.

The class reports a positive delivery action, a persistent temporary failure, or a permanent failure. The subject describes the likely source of a delivery problem, and the detail gives a more precise condition. When a client does not recognize a detail, it should still report the class and any recognized subject.
sections.plainLanguage: Read a status code from left to right: first the broad result, then the area involved, then the specific condition. A mail program can still report the parts it recognizes when it sees an unfamiliar code.

sections.title: The Classes and Subject Categories
sections.content:
Class 2 reports a positive delivery action. Class 4 reports a persistent temporary failure: the message is valid, but a temporary condition delayed or stopped delivery attempts, and a later attempt may succeed. Class 5 reports a permanent failure that is unlikely to be fixed by resending the message unchanged.

The subject applies across all three classes. The categories are other or undefined status, addressing, mailbox, destination mail system, network and routing, delivery protocol, message content or media, and security or policy. These categories help identify which part of the mail system or which party may be able to address a problem.
sections.plainLanguage: The first number says whether delivery succeeded, may succeed later, or needs a change before retrying. The middle number points to the area involved, such as an address, mailbox, network, or message content.

sections.title: Specific Conditions in the Detail Codes
sections.content:
The detail code refines the subject category. For example, X.1.1 means the destination mailbox does not exist, X.2.2 means the mailbox is full, and X.3.4 means the message is too large for the destination system. The class still determines whether the report describes success, a persistent temporary failure, or a permanent failure.

Other defined conditions include a bad connection (X.4.2), an inability to route (X.4.4), a required conversion that is not supported (X.6.3), and a cryptographic failure (X.7.5). Each detail code has a defined meaning and may be appropriate only for particular classes of result.
sections.plainLanguage: The last number gives the specific condition, such as a full mailbox or an unavailable route. The same detail category can have different meanings for a temporary and a permanent failure.

sections.title: Extending and Interpreting the Code Set
sections.content:
Only standards-track documents may extend the status-code space. Servers should send defined, registered codes, and mail systems should map local error conditions to the closest standard code. System-specific diagnostics should be carried separately rather than placed in a status code.

Published codes are not intended to be redefined or removed. A client must report a recognized class even when it does not recognize the subject. If it recognizes the subject but not the detail, it must report the general condition represented by the subject.
sections.plainLanguage: New standard codes can be added, but existing meanings stay stable. When a program sees a code it does not know, it reports the broadest part it does understand.

sections.title: Information Revealed by Detailed Reports
sections.content: The security consideration in RFC 3463 is that more precise status codes may disclose information about how an internal mail system is implemented. The document defines codes for security and policy conditions, but the codes report delivery status; they do not define a security mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: A detailed failure report can reveal more about the mail system that produced it. The status code reports a condition but does not protect the message.
